amphibious-frame.title: Frame material trade study
amphibious-frame.subtitle: Laser-cut sheet for an amphibious ring-frame robot
amphibious-frame.summary: Six sheet materials scored against the loads and environments an air–ground–water frame sees. Sealed birch plywood ranks first when the frame is cut in-house on a CO₂ laser; carbon-fiber plate takes over when machining can be outsourced or water exposure dominates.
amphibious-frame.question: Which sheet material should the laser-cut arms and decks be made from, given that the same frame has to fly, drive, and swim?
context: The arms and decks are thin plates loaded mostly in bending: motor thrust in flight, wheel and ground reactions when driving, and drag and buoyancy in water.
Every gram of frame costs flight time, so stiffness and strength are compared per unit mass, not in absolute terms.
The frame gets wet and takes hits — landings, curbs, rocks — so water durability and impact toughness matter as much as stiffness.
Parts are cut in-house on a CO₂ laser, which rules out some high-performance sheets unless machining is outsourced.
method: Stiffness and strength use Ashby's panel-in-bending indices for minimum mass at fixed length and width with free thickness: ∛E / ρ for stiffness and √σ / ρ for strength (E = flexural modulus in GPa, σ = flexural strength in MPa, ρ = density in g/cm³).

Index values are mapped linearly to a 1–5 score between the lowest and highest option. Water durability, impact toughness, manufacturability, and cost are scored 1–5 from datasheet behavior and shop constraints.
Totals are weighted sums. Three weight sets test whether the ranking survives a change in priorities.

criteria.name: In-house manufacturing
criteria.basis: Cuts cleanly and safely on a CO₂ laser

options.name: Birch plywood, sealed
options.note: Best stiffness per mass of any sheet here and cuts cleanly on a laser. Absorbs water and swells unless faces and cut edges are sealed; stiffness is lower across the face grain.

options.name: Cast acrylic (PMMA)
options.note: Waterproof and laser-friendly, but brittle — it cracks from notches and bolt holes on impact.

options.name: Acetal (POM)
options.note: Waterproof, very tough, and laser-cuttable with strong fume extraction. The most flexible option per unit mass.

options.name: Carbon-fiber plate
options.note: Strongest per unit mass and waterproof. Cannot be cut on a CO₂ laser; needs CNC routing with dust control, and edges can delaminate.

options.name: G10 glass-epoxy
options.note: Strong, tough, and waterproof, but heavy and abrasive to machine; not laser-cuttable.

options.name: Aluminum 5052-H32
options.note: Marine alloy that dents instead of cracking. Heaviest option and needs a waterjet, CNC, or fiber laser.

result: With the frame cut in-house, sealed birch plywood scores highest. No sheet material here beats wood on bending stiffness per unit mass, and it cuts quickly and cleanly on a CO₂ laser. Its weakness is water: faces and every cut edge need an epoxy or polyurethane seal.

Carbon-fiber plate is second at baseline and first under both alternative weightings — when machining is outsourced, or when water exposure dominates. The ranking therefore turns on the fabrication route, not on the material data.

Acetal is the best fully waterproof sheet that can still be laser cut, and tied with aluminum as the toughest in a crash, at the cost of the lowest stiffness per mass. Acrylic is ruled out by brittleness at bolt holes; G10 and aluminum carry too much mass for a flying frame.
amphibious-frame.recommendation: Prototype frames in sealed birch plywood for fast laser-cut iteration. Move the flight frame to carbon-fiber plate once CNC routing is available, and use acetal for splash-zone brackets and parts that take direct impacts.
limitations: Properties are typical datasheet values for ranking, not design allowables; grades and suppliers vary.
Plywood and carbon-fiber plate are anisotropic. Plywood's cross-grain stiffness can be roughly half the face-grain value, so arm layouts should follow the face grain.
The panel indices assume thickness is free to change. Fixed sheet gauges, fasteners, and joints shift real part masses.
sources: M. F. Ashby, Materials Selection in Mechanical Design, 5th ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2016 — panel-in-bending performance indices.
USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material, FPL-GTR-282, 2021 — wood and plywood properties and moisture behavior.
Manufacturer technical data sheets: cast acrylic (ACRYLITE GP), acetal homopolymer (Delrin 150), 3K twill carbon-fiber plate, NEMA grade G10 laminate, and aluminum 5052-H32.
